plan.title: Introduction to RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
learning_objectives: Explain what Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) means in simple words.
List the main reasons why RAG is useful for LLM answers.
Describe the five main steps of RAG: prepare, index, retrieve, augment, generate.
Explain common limits and mistakes about RAG, such as thinking it retrains the model.
plan.analogy: Analogy: Open-book exam in an Indian school. Mapping: The student is like the LLM because the student writes the final answer. The question paper is like the user query/question. The textbook or notes allowed in the exam are like the knowledge base. Searching the right page in the book is like retrieval. Copying the useful lines into rough work with the question is like augmentation, because extra information is added before answering. Writing the final answer in clear sentences is like generation. The page number or book name is like the source. The student’s memory does not permanently change just because they opened the book once; similarly, RAG does not permanently change the model weights.
plan.worked_example: Scenario: A sample college has a small knowledge base with notices. User question: “What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?” Retrieved information: Chunk 1 from Source: College Notice A: “Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August. Submit the form at the college office.” Chunk 2 from Source: College Notice B: “Sports day practice will start on 20 August.” Augmented prompt shown to the LLM: “Answer the question using only the information below. If the answer is not in the information, say you don’t know. Mention the source used. Information: [Source: College Notice A] Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August. Submit the form at the college office. [Source: College Notice B] Sports day practice will start on 20 August. Question: What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?” Final answer: “The last date to submit the scholarship form is 15 August. You should submit it at the college office. Source: College Notice A.” This example shows retrieval, augmentation, generation, and source use.

sections.heading: Hook: Like an Open-Book Exam
key_points: Ask the learner to imagine an open-book exam where they do not answer only from memory.
In an open-book exam, the student first finds the correct page, reads the useful lines, and then writes the answer.
RAG works in a similar way: before an AI model answers, it first gets useful information from documents.
Use only this one analogy throughout the lesson: open-book exam.

sections.heading: What RAG Is
key_points: Start with a very simple base idea: a Large Language Model is an AI model that can generate text answers.
Explain that a prompt is the text given to the model, such as instructions plus the user’s question.
Define Retrieval-Augmented Generation as a method for answering questions with an LLM.
In RAG, before the LLM answers, the system retrieves relevant pieces of information from an outside knowledge source.
The system adds those pieces of information to the prompt together with the question.
Then the LLM generates the answer using that information.

Break the name into three parts: Retrieval means finding and bringing back useful information; Augmentation means making the prompt bigger or better by adding information; Generation means creating the answer text.
Explain that a knowledge base is the outside collection of documents that RAG searches.
Use the open-book exam mapping: textbook/notes = knowledge base, finding useful page = retrieval, adding useful lines to the question = augmentation, writing final answer = generation.

sections.heading: Why RAG Matters
key_points: Explain knowledge cutoff: an LLM’s training data was collected only up to a certain date, so by itself it may not know recent notices, rules, prices, or scores.
Explain training data: the data used earlier to train the model.
RAG helps with updated information because it searches the knowledge base when the question is asked.
Explain hallucination: sometimes an LLM gives a fluent, confident answer that is false or made up.
RAG reduces hallucination because the model receives real, relevant text to answer from, but it does not remove hallucination completely.
Explain private or specific data: a general LLM did not see a company policy, hospital record, school timetable, college notice, or product manual unless that was in its training data.
RAG lets the model use such documents at answer time without retraining and without permanently learning them.
Explain trust: because RAG uses specific retrieved documents, the answer can show sources, so users can check them.
Explain cheaper and faster updates: changing documents in the knowledge base is usually cheaper and faster than retraining or fine-tuning a model.

sections.heading: How RAG Works Step by Step
key_points: Step 1: Prepare the knowledge. Collect useful documents such as web pages, PDF files, notices, manuals, policies, or articles.
Split long documents into small pieces called chunks, usually a few sentences to a few paragraphs long.
Small chunks help the system send only the most relevant parts of a long document to the model.
Some systems split by fixed number of tokens or characters; better systems split at natural boundaries like headings, paragraphs, or sentences.
Define token simply as a small piece of text used by the system.
Step 2: Index the chunks. Indexing means storing chunks in a way that makes them quick to search.
In a common method, each chunk is changed into an embedding: a list of numbers that represents meaning.
A vector is this kind of number list, and a vector database stores many embeddings with their text.
Some systems also use a keyword index, which finds chunks containing the same words as the question.
Step 3: Retrieve. When a user asks a question, the retriever searches the index for the most relevant chunks.
The user’s question can also be called a query.
With embeddings, the system compares the question embedding with stored chunk embeddings and finds the closest ones. This is similarity search.
Top-k means the system returns a small number of best-matching chunks, often between 3 and 10.
Step 4: Augment. Add the retrieved chunks to the prompt along with the user question and instructions.
Example instruction: answer only using the information provided, say ‘I don’t know’ if the answer is not there, and mention the source used.
Step 5: Generate. The LLM reads the whole augmented prompt and writes the answer using the retrieved chunks as main evidence.
Explain that in all these steps, the LLM’s model weights stay the same; RAG changes the prompt for one question, not the model itself.
Mention context window: there is a limit to how much retrieved text can be added to the prompt.

sections.heading: Worked Example: College Scholarship Notice
key_points: Set up a sample knowledge base with college notices, like the book/notes in the open-book exam analogy.
User asks the exact question: “What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?”
Prepare knowledge: the system has notices split into chunks, including Chunk 1 from College Notice A and Chunk 2 from College Notice B.
Retrieved Chunk 1: “Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August. Submit the form at the college office.”
Retrieved Chunk 2: “Sports day practice will start on 20 August.”
Show that Chunk 1 is relevant to the scholarship question; Chunk 2 is less relevant but may have been retrieved too.
Augment by building the prompt with instructions, retrieved chunks, and the user question.

Use this augmented prompt: “Answer the question using only the information below. If the answer is not in the information, say you don’t know. Mention the source used. Information: [Source: College Notice A] Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August. Submit the form at the college office. [Source: College Notice B] Sports day practice will start on 20 August. Question: What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?”
Generate the final answer: “The last date to submit the scholarship form is 15 August. You should submit it at the college office. Source: College Notice A.”
Point out which part came from which source, so the learner sees how trust is built.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Limits
key_points: Misconception 1: RAG retrains or permanently changes the model. Correct idea: false. Retrieved information is used only for that one answer; model weights do not change.
Misconception 2: RAG always gives correct answers. Correct idea: false. If the wrong chunks are retrieved, or documents are wrong or old, the answer can still be wrong.
Misconception 3: RAG is the same as fine-tuning. Correct idea: false. Fine-tuning changes the model itself; RAG only adds information to the prompt.
Misconception 4: Retrieving more text is always better. Correct idea: false. Irrelevant text can confuse the model, and the context window is limited.
Limit 1: Answer quality depends on retrieval quality. Wrong information in can lead to wrong answer out.
Limit 2: The knowledge base must be maintained. New documents must be added and old or wrong documents updated or removed.
Limit 3: The context window limits how much retrieved text can be added to the prompt.
Limit 4: The extra search step adds time and cost.
Limit 5: The model can still hallucinate or ignore the retrieved text.

sections.heading: Summary
key_points: RAG means retrieve, augment, generate.
It is like an open-book exam: find the right information first, add it to the question, then write the answer.
RAG helps when information is recent, private, specific, or needs sources.
The five main steps are: prepare knowledge, index chunks, retrieve relevant chunks, augment the prompt, and generate the answer.
RAG does not retrain the LLM or permanently change model weights.
RAG improves answers, but it does not guarantee correctness; the knowledge base and retrieval quality are very important.

sections.heading: Hook: Like an Open-Book Exam
sections.body_markdown:
Imagine an open-book exam in your school. You do not answer only from memory. You read the question. Then you find the right page in your book. You copy useful lines in rough work. Then you write the final answer.

**Artificial Intelligence** [कृत्रिम बुद्धि] means computer programs that do tasks needing human thinking. **Retrieval-Augmented Generation** [जानकारी खोजकर, उसे जोड़कर जवाब बनाने का तरीका] is similar to that exam. The AI does not answer only from memory. It first finds useful information from documents. Then it uses that information to write the answer.

Here is the map. The student is like the AI model. The question paper is like your question. The textbook is like the documents. Finding the right page is **retrieval**. Adding useful lines to rough work is **augmentation**. Writing the final answer is **generation**. The page or book name is the **source**.

sections.heading: What RAG Is
sections.body_markdown:
A **Large Language Model** [बड़ा भाषा मॉडल], or LLM, is an AI model that can understand and write language. A **prompt** [मॉडल को दिया गया सवाल और निर्देश] is the text given to the model. It can include instructions and your question.

**Retrieval** [खोजकर लाना] means finding useful information and bringing it back. **Augmentation** [कुछ जोड़कर बढ़ाना] means adding useful information to make the prompt better. **Generation** [बनाना, रचना] means creating new text, like an answer.

So, RAG has a simple meaning. Before the LLM answers, the system finds useful outside information. It adds that information to the prompt with your question. Then the LLM writes the answer using that information.

A **knowledge base** [जानकारी का भंडार] is the document collection that RAG searches. It can contain web pages, college notices, policies, manuals, or articles. It is separate from the LLM. You can update it without changing the model.

In the exam map, the textbook is the knowledge base. Finding the page is retrieval. Adding lines to the question is augmentation. Writing the answer is generation.

sections.heading: Why RAG Matters
sections.body_markdown:
First, RAG helps with new information. **Training data** [प्रशिक्षण डेटा] is the text an AI model learned from. A **knowledge cutoff** [जानकारी की आखिरी तारीख] is the last date of that learned information. By itself, an LLM may not know a notice published after that date. The result can be a wrong answer about a new rule.

RAG can search the knowledge base when you ask. If the knowledge base is updated, the answer can use current text. For example, a college can add a new exam notice. Then students can ask about it.

Second, RAG helps reduce **hallucination** [मनगढ़ंत जवाब]. Hallucination means an AI gives a false answer that sounds correct. This can mislead a student about a deadline. RAG gives the LLM real text to use. This reduces the chance of a made-up answer. It does not remove the risk fully.

Third, RAG helps with private or specific documents. A general LLM may not have your school timetable or shop return policy. With RAG, those documents can be searched at answer time. The LLM does not permanently learn them.

Fourth, RAG can build trust. A **source** [स्रोत] is the place where information came from. A RAG answer can show the source. Then you can check the notice yourself.

Fifth, updates can be easier. **Fine-tuning** [मॉडल को दोबारा सिखाना] means training a model again so the model itself changes. Adding documents to a knowledge base is usually cheaper and faster than fine-tuning or retraining.

sections.heading: How RAG Works Step by Step
sections.body_markdown:
RAG has five main steps.

Step 1 is prepare the knowledge. The system collects useful documents. It may collect web pages, files, notices, manuals, policies, or articles. Long documents are split into chunks. A **chunk** [टुकड़ा] is a small piece of a long document. It is often a few sentences or paragraphs. Small chunks help send only useful parts to the LLM.

Some systems split text by **tokens**. A **token** [शब्द का छोटा टुकड़ा] is a small piece of text an LLM reads. Some systems split by characters. Better systems often split at headings, paragraphs, or sentences.

Step 2 is index the chunks. An **index** [खोजने के लिए बनी सूची] is an organised store that makes search fast. In a common method, each chunk becomes an **embedding**. An **embedding** [अर्थ बताने वाली संख्याओं की सूची] is a list of numbers that shows meaning. A **vector** [संख्याओं की सूची] is a list of numbers. A **vector database** [संख्याओं की सूचियों का डेटाबेस] stores embeddings with their text. Some systems also use **keyword search**. **Keyword search** [शब्दों से खोज] finds text with the same words as the question.

Step 3 is retrieve. A **retriever** [खोजकर लाने वाला हिस्सा] is the part that searches and returns chunks. A **query** [सवाल या खोज] is your question for search. With embeddings, the query also becomes an embedding. **Similarity search** [मिलती-जुलती चीज़ खोजना] finds chunks closest in meaning to the query. **Top-k** [सबसे मिलते-जुलते कुछ नतीजे] means the best matching chunks returned. Often, this is between 3 and 10 chunks.

Step 4 is augment. The system adds the retrieved chunks to the prompt. It also adds your question and instructions. One instruction can say, “Use only the given information.” Another can say, “Say you do not know if it is not there.”

Step 5 is generate. The LLM reads the full augmented prompt. It writes the answer using the retrieved chunks. It can also mention the source.

The model itself does not change in these steps. **Model weights** [मॉडल के अंदर सीखी हुई संख्याएँ] are numbers inside the model that store what it learned. RAG does not retrain the LLM. It only changes the prompt for one question.

There is one more limit here. A **context window** [एक बार में पढ़ने की सीमा] is how much text an LLM can read at one time. Too much retrieved text may not fit. Extra unrelated text can also distract the model.

sections.heading: Worked Example: College Scholarship Notice
sections.body_markdown:
Let us use a sample college knowledge base. It is like the textbook in the open-book exam.

User question: “What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?”

Step 1, prepare. The system has college notices split into chunks.

Chunk 1 is from Source: College Notice A.

“Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August. Submit the form at the college office.”

Chunk 2 is from Source: College Notice B.

“Sports day practice will start on 20 August.”

Step 2, index. The system stores these chunks for fast search. It may store embeddings for their meanings.

Step 3, retrieve. The retriever searches for the user question. Chunk 1 matches the scholarship question. Chunk 2 is less useful, but it may also be returned.

Step 4, augment. The system builds this prompt for the LLM:

“Answer the question using only the information below.
If the answer is not in the information, say you don’t know.
Mention the source used.
Information:
[Source: College Notice A]
Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August.
Submit the form at the college office.
[Source: College Notice B]
Sports day practice will start on 20 August.
Question: What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?”

Step 5, generate. The LLM writes the final answer:

“The last date to submit the scholarship form is 15 August. You should submit it at the college office. Source: College Notice A.”

Notice how the answer uses College Notice A. It ignores the sports day line. You can check the source if needed.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Limits
sections.body_markdown:
Misconception 1: RAG retrains the model. This is false. RAG uses found information only for that one answer. Model weights do not change.

Misconception 2: RAG is the same as fine-tuning. This is false. Fine-tuning changes the model itself. RAG only adds information to the prompt.

Misconception 3: RAG always gives correct answers. This is false. Wrong chunks can be retrieved. Documents can also be old or wrong. Then the answer can still be wrong.

Misconception 4: More text is always better. This is false. The context window is limited. Unrelated text can confuse the model.

RAG has limits. Answer quality depends on retrieval quality. The knowledge base must be maintained. New documents must be added. Old or wrong documents should be updated or removed. The extra search step can add time and cost. The model can still hallucinate or ignore the retrieved text.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body_markdown:
RAG means retrieve, augment, and generate. It is like an open-book exam. You find the right information first. You add it with the question. Then the answer is written.

RAG helps with new, private, and specific information. It can reduce hallucination. It can show sources for checking. Its five steps are prepare, index, retrieve, augment, and generate.

RAG does not retrain the LLM. It does not permanently change model weights. It improves answers, but it does not guarantee correctness. The knowledge base and retrieval quality matter a lot.

sections.heading: Hook: A Direct First Picture
sections.body_markdown:
When you ask an AI system a question, it may need facts from documents. It should not answer only from memory.

**Artificial Intelligence** [कृत्रिम बुद्धि] means computer programs that do tasks needing human thinking. **Retrieval-Augmented Generation** [जानकारी खोजकर, उसे जोड़कर जवाब बनाने का तरीका] is a method for AI answers.

In this method, the system first finds useful information from documents. Then it adds that information to the question. After that, the AI writes the answer.

The document is the place that stores facts. The question is what you ask. The found text is the extra help. The final written text is the answer. The page or document name is the **source**.

sections.heading: What RAG Is
sections.body_markdown:
A **Large Language Model** [बड़ा भाषा मॉडल], or LLM, is an AI model that can understand and write language. A **prompt** [मॉडल को दिया गया सवाल और निर्देश] is the text given to the model. It can include instructions and your question.

**Retrieval** [खोजकर लाना] means finding useful information and bringing it back. **Augmentation** [कुछ जोड़कर बढ़ाना] means adding useful information to make the prompt better. **Generation** [बनाना, रचना] means creating new text, like an answer.

So, RAG has a simple meaning. Before the LLM answers, the system finds useful outside information. It adds that information to the prompt with your question. Then the LLM writes the answer using that information.

A **knowledge base** [जानकारी का भंडार] is the document collection that RAG searches. It can contain web pages, college notices, policies, manuals, or articles. It is separate from the LLM. You can update it without changing the model.

Use a school exam comparison to remember the parts. In this comparison, a textbook represents the knowledge base. Finding the correct page represents retrieval. Adding useful lines to the question represents augmentation. Writing the final answer represents generation.

sections.heading: Why RAG Matters
sections.body_markdown:
First, RAG helps with new information. **Training data** [प्रशिक्षण डेटा] is the text an AI model learned from. A **knowledge cutoff** [जानकारी की आखिरी तारीख] is the last date of that learned information. By itself, an LLM may not know a notice published after that date. The result can be a wrong answer about a new rule.

RAG can search the knowledge base when you ask. If the knowledge base is updated, the answer can use current text. For example, a college can add a new exam notice. Then students can ask about it.

Second, RAG helps reduce **hallucination** [मनगढ़ंत जवाब]. Hallucination means an AI gives a false answer that sounds correct. This can mislead a student about a deadline. RAG gives the LLM real text to use. This reduces the chance of a made-up answer. It does not remove the risk fully.

Third, RAG helps with private or specific documents. A general LLM may not have your school timetable or shop return policy. With RAG, those documents can be searched at answer time. The LLM does not permanently learn them.

Fourth, RAG can build trust. A **source** [स्रोत] is the place where information came from. A RAG answer can show the source. Then you can check the notice yourself.

Fifth, updates can be easier. **Fine-tuning** [मॉडल को दोबारा सिखाना] means training a model again so the model itself changes. Adding documents to a knowledge base is usually cheaper and faster than fine-tuning or retraining.

sections.heading: How RAG Works Step by Step
sections.body_markdown:
RAG has five main steps.

Step 1 is prepare the knowledge. The system collects useful documents. It may collect web pages, files, notices, manuals, policies, or articles. Long documents are split into chunks. A **chunk** [टुकड़ा] is a small piece of a long document. It is often a few sentences or paragraphs. Small chunks help send only useful parts to the LLM.

Some systems split text by **tokens**. A **token** [शब्द का छोटा टुकड़ा] is a small piece of text an LLM reads. Some systems split by characters. Better systems often split at headings, paragraphs, or sentences.

Step 2 is index the chunks. An **index** [खोजने के लिए बनी सूची] is an organised store that makes search fast. In a common method, each chunk becomes an **embedding**. An **embedding** [अर्थ बताने वाली संख्याओं की सूची] is a list of numbers that shows meaning. A **vector** [संख्याओं की सूची] is a list of numbers. A **vector database** [संख्याओं की सूचियों का डेटाबेस] stores embeddings with their text. Some systems also use **keyword search**. **Keyword search** [शब्दों से खोज] finds text with the same words as the question.

Step 3 is retrieve. A **retriever** [खोजकर लाने वाला हिस्सा] is the part that searches and returns chunks. A **query** [सवाल या खोज] is your question for search. With embeddings, the query also becomes an embedding. **Similarity search** [मिलती-जुलती चीज़ खोजना] finds chunks closest in meaning to the query. **Top-k** [सबसे मिलते-जुलते कुछ नतीजे] means the best matching chunks returned. Often, this is between 3 and 10 chunks.

Step 4 is augment. The system adds the retrieved chunks to the prompt. It also adds your question and instructions. One instruction can say, “Use only the given information.” Another can say, “Say you do not know if it is not there.”

Step 5 is generate. The LLM reads the full augmented prompt. It writes the answer using the retrieved chunks. It can also mention the source.

The model itself does not change in these steps. **Model weights** [मॉडल के अंदर सीखी हुई संख्याएँ] are numbers inside the model that store what it learned. RAG does not retrain the LLM. It only changes the prompt for one question.

There is one more limit here. A **context window** [एक बार में पढ़ने की सीमा] is how much text an LLM can read at one time. Too much retrieved text may not fit. Extra unrelated text can also distract the model.

sections.heading: Worked Example: College Scholarship Notice
sections.body_markdown:
Let us use a sample college knowledge base. The college notices are the documents that the system searches.

User question: “What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?”

Step 1, prepare. The system has college notices split into chunks.

Chunk 1 is from Source: College Notice A.

“Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August. Submit the form at the college office.”

Chunk 2 is from Source: College Notice B.

“Sports day practice will start on 20 August.”

Step 2, index. The system stores these chunks for fast search. It may store embeddings for their meanings.

Step 3, retrieve. The retriever searches for the user question. Chunk 1 matches the scholarship question. Chunk 2 is less useful, but it may also be returned.

Step 4, augment. The system builds this prompt for the LLM:

“Answer the question using only the information below.
If the answer is not in the information, say you don’t know.
Mention the source used.
Information:
[Source: College Notice A]
Scholarship form submission: Students must submit the scholarship form by 15 August.
Submit the form at the college office.
[Source: College Notice B]
Sports day practice will start on 20 August.
Question: What is the last date to submit the scholarship form, and where should I submit it?”

Step 5, generate. The LLM writes the final answer:

“The last date to submit the scholarship form is 15 August. You should submit it at the college office. Source: College Notice A.”

Notice how the answer uses College Notice A. It ignores the sports day line. You can check the source if needed.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Limits
sections.body_markdown:
Misconception 1: RAG retrains the model. This is false. RAG uses found information only for that one answer. Model weights do not change.

Misconception 2: RAG is the same as fine-tuning. This is false. Fine-tuning changes the model itself. RAG only adds information to the prompt.

Misconception 3: RAG always gives correct answers. This is false. Wrong chunks can be retrieved. Documents can also be old or wrong. Then the answer can still be wrong.

Misconception 4: More text is always better. This is false. The context window is limited. Unrelated text can confuse the model.

RAG has limits. Answer quality depends on retrieval quality. The knowledge base must be maintained. New documents must be added. Old or wrong documents should be updated or removed. The extra search step can add time and cost. The model can still hallucinate or ignore the retrieved text.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body_markdown:
RAG means retrieve, augment, and generate. The system finds the right information first. It adds the information with the question. Then the answer is written.

RAG helps with new, private, and specific information. It can reduce hallucination. It can show sources for checking. Its five steps are prepare, index, retrieve, augment, and generate.

RAG does not retrain the LLM. It does not permanently change model weights. It improves answers, but it does not guarantee correctness. The knowledge base and retrieval quality matter a lot.
